works.abstract: The vexing error of excess variance in the sizing of single particles degrades accuracy in applications ranging from quality control of nanoparticle products to hazard assessment of nanoplastic byproducts. The particular importance of lipid nanoparticles for vaccine and medicine delivery motivates this comment on a publication$^{\textrm{1}}$ in ACS Nano. In ref 1, the benchmark measurements of a nanoparticle standard manifest large errors of the size distribution that contradict the claim of validation. Such errors can bias the correlation of fluorescence intensity as an optical proxy for the molecular loading of lipid nanoparticles and give misleading insights from power-law models of intensity$-$size data. Looking forward, measurement error models have the potential to address this widespread issue.
works.title: Letter to the Editor Concerning “Simultaneous, Single-Particle Measurements of Size and Loading Give Insights into the Structure of Drug-Delivery Nanoparticles”

works.abstract: Correlative microscopy combines complementary images from multiple instruments in a synergistic analysis of nanoscale structures and properties. However, the correlation of disparate images at random locations across a wide field is challenging, limiting measurement throughput and statistical sampling. Major challenges include microscopy position errors and sample preparation issues [1,2]. Meeting both challenges would enhance correlative microscopy for many applications. To solve this problem, we introduce correlative microscopy arrays, featuring square arrays of nanoscale fiducials that we design for compatibility with multiple microscopy methods and suspension deposition processes. We fabricate prototype arrays in silicon (100) using electron beam lithography and reactive ion etching, forming robust and reusable imaging substrates. We etch the fiducials into the substrate to reduce interference with suspension deposition and to present a different feature polarity in comparison to nanoparticles on top of the substrate, facilitating image interpretation. As well, fiducial arrays provide reference positions for magnification calibration and distortion correction for each instrument, enabling programmatic registration of image data with minimal error [3]. In this way, we can achieve a novel integration of standard and sample for in situ correlative calibration. We apply a prototype array in an initial study of the dependence of fluorescence intensity on the spherical diameter of polystyrene nanoparticles, which commonly serve as size standards and may serve as intensity standards in benchmark tests of nanomedicine and nanoplastic measurements. However, the intensity–size trend is poorly understood and subject to bias due to sizing errors [4], requiring correlative metrology to obtain a reference trend. Accordingly, we perform correlative optical microscopy (Figure 1a,b) and atomic force microscopy (Figure 1c,d) on single nanoparticles, with corresponding corrections for intensity non-uniformity and height non-linearity to improve accuracy. In an initial sizing analysis, we model the nanoparticle image as a sphere (Figure 1d, dotted circle), accounting for the convolution artifact of the probe tip, with spherical height corresponding to nanoparticle diameter. An evaluation of total sizing uncertainty is ongoing. A primary component of sizing uncertainty is calibration uncertainty for scanner non-linearity in the vertical direction, which we report in Figure 1d. For a small statistical sample of 15 nanoparticles, we find the semi-quantitative agreement of particle diameters in a comparison of manufacturer specifications resulting from transmission electron microscopy and our measurement results from atomic force microscopy (Table 1). Future analysis of larger statistical samples will allow a fully quantitative comparison of distributional moments and uncertainties. These initial results allow a least-squares fit of a power-law model to the intensity–diameter trend, yielding an apparent exponent of approximately 2.5 (Figure 1e). However, this preliminary statistical analysis does not yet account for attenuation bias of the power-law exponent due to independent variable uncertainty, which likely causes a significant underestimate of the true exponent. A measurement error model accounting for total sizing uncertainty will allow correction of the apparent exponent [4]. Building on this initial dataset (Figure 1e), we aim to extend our novel methodology across a broad range of nanoparticle samples. Scaling up such a correlative measurement to large counts of single nanoparticles is challenging due to the long scan times of atomic force microscopy. Making use of the array reference positions, we introduce an accurate targeting methodology, guiding the atomic force microscope toward features of interest using optical localization data. This methodology avoids featureless regions and preserves high resolution of target features, improving the resolution–throughput tradespace. Initial tests of the inaccurate targeting of array features indicate that relatively large regions of up to a few micrometers may be necessary to tolerate position errors and hit target features across the full scan field (Figure 2). The spatial variation and experimental repeatability of position errors remain under investigation. A representative pattern of position errors indicates that angular misalignment of the array and microscope axes, scale-factor error, and scan-field distortion are all potential limits of accuracy (Figure 2). Accordingly, angular alignment calibration, scale-factor calibration, and scan-field distortion correction will all reduce position errors to enable accurate targeting of features within minimal tolerance regions. In turn, this capability will maximize the throughput of correlative microscopy, enabling measurements of many single nanoparticles to obtain reliable reference data, and for other applications [5]. (a) Composite micrograph combining (white) darkfield and (green) fluorescence imaging modes of the same optical microscope, showing spherical polystyrene nanoparticles on a correlative microscopy array. Peripheral characters label fiducial positions. (b) Composite optical micrograph showing a region of interest, corresponding to the orange square in panel (a). (c) Atomic force micrograph showing a region of interest, corresponding to the orange dashed square in panels (a) and (b). (d) Atomic force micrograph profile showing the different vertical-position polarities of a fiducial and a nanoparticle from (c). (e) Scatter plot showing preliminary data for the apparent dependence of fluorescence intensity on spherical diameter. Initial diameter uncertainties are 68% coverage intervals. Intensity uncertainties are smaller than the data markers. The solid green line shows the least-squares estimate for a power-law model. Spatial map showing representative position errors from initial tests targeting array features across the full scan field of an atomic force microscope. Dots indicate reference positions of a correlative microscopy array. Arrows depict representative position errors, with colors indicating magnitude. For ease of visualization, we lengthen the arrows beyond the lateral position scale. Initial comparison of particle diameter distributions from different microscopy methods.
works.title: Toward Accurate Targeting in Correlative Microscopy
